title: Topological Signatures of Hardness and Structural Order in Network-Forming Materials
authors: Yair Augusto Gutiérrez Fosado, Ayobami Daramola, Davide Marenduzzo, Ciprian G. Pruteanu
abstract: Understanding how the topology of network forming materials influences their physical properties remains a longstanding challenge. Here, we investigate the topology of experimentally compatible atomistic models of amorphous silica together with the crystalline polymorphs cristobalite and quartz. By comparing multiple atomistic models of amorphous silica that equally reproduce neutron-scattering data, we show that different microscopic descriptions can imply different topological interpretations of glass stability. To characterize the network beyond conventional geometric descriptors, we introduce the linking valence, which quantifies the average number of topological links per network loop. This topological descriptor separates silica into two distinct classes: the mechanically harder quartz exhibit values more than an order of magnitude larger than those of amorphous silica and cristobalite, despite their common tetrahedral building blocks. Spectral analysis of the loop-linking networks provides a complementary distinction, separating amorphous from crystalline phases and revealing differences in the long-range organization of topological constraints. These results establish topological linking as a new framework for connecting the structure and physical properties of network-forming materials.
summary: This work develops a topological framework using the 'linking valence' to characterize network-forming materials like silica. By analyzing the linking between structural loops, the authors successfully distinguish between amorphous and crystalline phases, correlating topological constraints with mechanical hardness. This establishes linking as a powerful new tool for connecting structure and physical properties in disordered solids.
main_problem: The study aims to move beyond conventional geometric descriptors to understand how the topology of network-forming materials dictates their physical properties, particularly mechanical hardness.
main_result: The introduction of the linking valence successfully separates silica phases into distinct topological classes, correlating high linking values with mechanically harder crystalline phases like quartz.
method: The authors characterize the network by constructing a graph from atomic bonds and analyzing the topology using the Gauss linking number to define a 'linking valence' descriptor.
model_or_system: The research focuses on network-forming materials, specifically amorphous silica and its crystalline polymorphs (quartz, cristobalite), and amorphous ice, modeled using atomistic simulations constrained by neutron-scattering data.
key_observables: Linking valence (Z), Gauss linking number, graph Laplacian spectrum, and Inverse Participation Ratio (IPR).
important_parameters: The linking valence $Z$ is the key descriptor, which varies significantly based on the charge assignment used in the atomistic model.
main_assumptions: The topological picture is highly sensitive to the underlying atomistic model (e.g., charge assignment) used to define the network structure.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the AIASSE workflow, show the separation of silica phases based on linking valence vs. loop size, and present spectral analysis (Laplacian spectra and IPR) comparing different amorphous and crystalline states.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the inadequacy of geometric descriptors to introducing the linking valence, demonstrating its ability to distinguish phases, and finally complementing this with spectral analysis (Laplacian/IPR) to provide a comprehensive topological fingerprint.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter structure, the use of graph theory, spectral analysis (Laplacian), and localization measures (IPR) to characterize structural order shares methodological overlap with analyzing complex quantum many-body systems or disordered quantum states.

FIG. 2. Topological analysis of silica networks. (a) Average number of loops per particle, Nloops/M, as a function of the maximum loop size lmax for amorphous silica, α- and β-cristobalite, and α- and β-quartz. The black dashed line shows the exponential scaling Nloops/M ∝exp(0.35 lmax). (b) Linking valence, Z = L/Nloops, as a function of lmax. The black dashed line shows the scaling Z ∝exp(0.82 lmax). (c-e) Representative examples of loops and mutually linked loops identified in different phases.

FIG. 3. Global organization of topological constraints. (a)-(d) Linking matrices Lkij for different silica phases, all obtained using data with lmax = 28. (e) Laplacian eigenvalue spectra for the amorphous silica networks generated using optimized, reduced, and standard charge assignments. All three amorphous networks exhibit broad, monotonically decaying spectra. Interestingly, the decay rate of the amorphous network with standard-charge is significantly different, and larger, than those of the reduced and optimized charges, showing that quantum mechanics information leads to topologically different networks.
